option.value: Session 2: A Closer Look at Investigations Curriculum Units

slidetranscripts.slidetranscript:
Welcome to A Closer Look at Investigations Curriculum Units-the second session of the Investigations in Number, Data, and Space for the Common Core: Product Implementation Essentials Fused Online Course. This session should take you approximately 75 minutes to complete.

You’ll need your Participant Workbook and your Core Curriculum Package for this session. Pause the session while you gather these resources.

Before you begin, review what you learned in Session 1.

You learned about the organization of the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics-or the CCSSM. You explored how the CCSSM are integrated into Investigations for the Common Core.

You learned how to use your Core Curriculum Package to fully align your mathematics instruction to the CCSSM.

Finally, you focused deeply on the Standards for Mathematical Practice and learned how these standards are embedded in the fabric of Investigations.

Now, take a look at the Session 2 Objectives.

During this session, you will

·implement the instructional components of a Curriculum Unit for optimal student learning and mathematical proficiency; and

·utilize Investigations resources in your classroom to personalize and differentiate instruction for your students.

By now, you should have examined the contents in your Core Curriculum Package. During this session, you will explore these components in greater depth and learn how to use specific differentiation resources in your instruction to target your students’ learning needs.

Now, watch a video that summarizes the organization of an Investigations Curriculum Unit.

Begin by opening one of your Curriculum Units to follow along.

The Curriculum Unit is your main teaching tool. It’s your blueprint for the sequence and purpose of the daily lessons; it also contains guidelines for assessment, suggestions for differentiating instruction, and professional development materials to support your teaching.

Investigations is meant to be implemented in daily, one-hour sessions¾or as you may refer to them, daily lessons¾in addition to brief Ten-Minute Math activities that are spread throughout the day.

A chart called Today’s Plan appears at the beginning of each session and lays out the suggested pacing for the activities in that one-hour session. While you may need to adapt this structure to your particular classroom needs, be aware that it is important to move through all of the activities as they are carefully designed to offer continued work on the key mathematical ideas. It is also essential that you allow time for class discussions, where students have an opportunity to articulate their own ideas, compare solutions, and consolidate understanding.

Take a look at an overview of the activity features in each session.

If you would like to learn more about each feature, pause the video, and click the icons on the diagram to view an example of each session feature in the Curriculum Unit.

One guiding principle of Investigations is to provide support that helps teachers
improve their own understanding of the mathematics that they teach and the learning that they observe in their students.

The Professional Development section in the back of each Curriculum Unit contains a collection of Teacher Notes and Dialogue Boxes that help teachers assess and understand how their students learn mathematics.

Consider the following classroom scene from a Grade 5 Teacher Note in Unit 1:

“Cecelia and Talisha made a rectangle from 24 tiles to solve a number puzzle. The rectangle is 6 tiles across and 4 tiles down. Its dimensions are 4 by 6.

Talisha used a clue that the number is a multiple of 6. When we discussed the multiples of 6, some people said 2 and 3 and some other people said 6, 12, 18, 24, and 30. Which are factors of 6, and which are multiples of 6?”

The teacher, Mrs. Marsh, just taught her students about multiples, and she wonders if some of her students either don’t understand the difference between factors and multiples or if their use of correct terms does not match their understanding.

The Professional Development reference in the side bar led Mrs. Marsh to the Teacher Note essay, “Using Mathematical Vocabulary.”

How will this Teacher Note help Mrs. Marsh in her teaching?

Mrs. Marsh learned teaching strategies to help her students think about precise mathematical language, and to help her better assess her students’ level of understanding.

Teacher Notes are essays that provide further practical information about the mathematics content and how students learn it. Many of the notes were written in response to questions from teachers or to discuss important issues that arose in field-test classrooms. They offer teachers help with thinking about mathematical ideas that may be unfamiliar to them; they also provide guidance for observing and assessing students' work.

Dialogue Boxes reflect classroom scenarios that relate to the activities of the unit and depict actual teacher-student interactions. They offer examples of how students typically express their mathematical ideas, what issues and confusions arise in their thinking, and how some teachers have chosen to guide particular class discussions.

It’s time to Pause and Reflect! Before you continue, please respond to the Session 2 Pause and Reflect question in the Participant Workbook.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.

Every classroom includes a range of learners-students who struggle with or excel in certain areas of mathematics, students with particular learning needs, and students who are English language learners.

An important idea in teaching a range of learners is to recognize that all learners are accountable for mastering the same standards.

According to the Investigations in Number, Data and Space: Grade 4 Investigations and the Common Core State Standards resource book, “The Common Core State Standards insist that all students must be supported in their learning so they can meet all of the standards. Differentiating instruction helps students achieve this goal.”

Basia Hall, a math educator and Pearson author stated the following: “Differentiated instruction does not change what is taught; it changes how it is taught.”

How can Investigations resources support you in differentiating instruction so that every type of learner has the opportunity to understand and master the mathematical concepts?

By now, you should have examined the contents in your Core Curriculum Package. During this session, you will explore these components in greater depth and learn how to use specific differentiation resources in your instruction to target your students’ learning needs.

Now, you’ll have a chance to watch part of an Investigations for the Common Core lesson and observe how an Investigations teacher implements some of the Investigations lesson features that you just learned about. After watching the video, you will be asked to respond to two reflection questions in your Participant Workbook.

Respond to the following video reflection questions in your Participant Workbook.

How does the teacher use the Discussion Activity to develop students’ understanding of the Math Focus Points?

Identify one Investigations feature or resource-in addition to the Discussion Activity-that the teacher uses to support students’ understanding of the concept. Describe how she incorporates this resource into instruction.

You've explored the instructional resources in your Core Curriculum Package and focused on resources that support differentiated instruction. Listen as an Investigations teacher discusses how she utilizes her Investigations resources to support the range of learners in her classroom.

Now you’ll have a chance to learn about the individual students in your classroom. It is important to know students’ need and plan the strategies that support their learning.

Use the graphic organizer in the Participant Workbook to record your student observations and responses. The work you do for this assignment will help you complete the final assignment and respond to the Discussion Board.

Refer to the directions in the Participant Workbook.

When you’re ready to move on, click Next.
It’s time to share your thoughts with your peers! Go to the Discussion Board and respond to the Session 2 Discussion Board questions as you reflect on this session.

Let’s review what you have learned in this session.

You looked at the structure of a Curriculum Unit and learned about the features and activities that are part of an Investigations session.

You explored the Professional Development resources and saw how the Professional Development pages support the Math Focus Points.

Then, you watched a video that showcased the implementation of some of the Investigations features that you have just explored.

Finally, you had an opportunity to survey the range of learners in your classroom and identify useful resources to support their learning needs.

In the next session, you’ll learn how an active mathematics classroom enhances learning and increases understanding through games and rich mathematical discussions.

Be sure to complete the following tasks before beginning Self-Paced Session 3.


Read the article, “Classroom Influences on Learning” in your Participant Workbook.

Continue filling out the Lesson Plan Implementation graphic organizer for your final assignment. The completed implementation plan is due before Session 5.

Read and post your responses to the Session 2 Discussion Board.


Respond to two Discussion Board posts from other participants.

Now, show what you know! Visit the course homepage to take the assessment for Session 2.

We’ll see you again in Session 3!
